mainEntity.name: Can wearing a broken denture damage my gums?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, wearing a broken denture can cause physical damage to the gums and other soft tissues inside the mouth. Fractured acrylic resin can develop sharp edges that cut or abrade the delicate mucous membrane lining. Even without visible sharp edges, a denture that no longer fits correctly following a break may create uneven pressure that leads to soreness, ulcers, or inflammation. It is generally advisable to seek dental assessment before continuing to wear a damaged denture, particularly if you are already experiencing discomfort.

mainEntity.name: How long should a mouth sore from a denture take to heal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Minor irritation or small sores caused by a new denture or recent adjustment often settle within one to two weeks, provided the source of irritation is removed or corrected. If a sore persists beyond two weeks, does not appear to be healing, or is growing in size, it is important to have it professionally assessed. Persistent oral lesions should not be left uninvestigated, as a dental professional will want to confirm the cause and ensure appropriate management.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to use denture adhesive if my denture no longer fits well?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture adhesive can offer temporary additional stability for minor fit issues, but it is not a long-term solution for a denture that has significantly changed in fit. Relying on adhesive as a substitute for professional adjustment or relining may mask underlying changes in the jaw or gum tissue that require attention. If your denture has suddenly become loose following damage, a dental assessment is the most appropriate first step rather than increasing adhesive use.

mainEntity.name: What is denture stomatitis and how does it relate to mouth sores?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture stomatitis is a common condition in denture wearers characterised by redness, soreness, and sometimes inflammation of the mucous membrane beneath the denture — particularly under upper dentures on the palate. It is often associated with an overgrowth of Candida albicans (a naturally occurring fungal organism), which can thrive in the warm, moist environment beneath a denture. It is more common when dentures are worn continuously without removal. Treatment typically involves improved hygiene practices and, where appropriate, antifungal medication prescribed following clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat and drink normally if my denture has a small crack?

acceptedAnswer.text: A small crack in a denture can worsen quickly under the forces of eating. Continuing to wear a cracked denture without repair may allow the fracture to spread, eventually causing the denture to break entirely. Additionally, a cracked surface may harbour bacteria, increasing hygiene concerns. While waiting for a professional appointment, it may be advisable to soften your diet and avoid foods that require heavy chewing. Your dental professional can advise on the safest course of action for your specific situation.

mainEntity.name: When should I consider having my denture relined or replaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dentures generally require assessment and possible adjustment over time, as the jaw bone and gum tissue can change in shape and volume following tooth loss. Signs that relining or replacement may be needed include a noticeable change in fit, increased movement of the denture during eating or speaking, recurring sore spots, or visible wear on the denture teeth. Your dental professional can assess whether relining, rebasing, or a new denture would be most appropriate based on the current condition of both the appliance and your oral tissues.
